sections.b:
Nearly every story in 1 Chronicles 10–20 has a twin in 1 or 2 Samuel: Saul's death (1 Samuel 31), the anointing at Hebron and the capture of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5), the hero list (2 Samuel 23), the ark (2 Samuel 6), Nathan's oracle (2 Samuel 7), and the wars (2 Samuel 8; 10; 12; 21). What Chronicles adds is just as telling: the verdict on Saul (10:13–14), the men who joined David (12), the Levites and singers (15:1–24; 16:4–42). It also moves the first ark story before the Philistine wars.

The comparison shows all three kinds of difference. Some changes are the Chronicler's own, such as "in my house and in my kingdom" (17:14) or the silence about Bathsheba (20:1). Some come from a Samuel text unlike the Masoretic one: Chronicles often agrees with the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a or the Greek (13:6; 13:10; 15:26; 18:4). Some are copying slips in one book or the other (11:13; 18:6; 20:3).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:1–14; 1 Chronicles 11:1–47; 1 Chronicles 13:1–14; 1 Chronicles 17:1–27; 1 Chronicles 20:1–8; 1 Samuel 31:1–13; 2 Samuel 5:1–25; 2 Samuel 6:1–23; 2 Samuel 7:1–29; 2 Samuel 23:8–39

common: Chronicles used a form of Samuel close to, but not identical with, the Masoretic Text.
uncommon: Some scholars (A. Graeme Auld) argue that Samuel–Kings and Chronicles both drew on an older shared story, so Chronicles did not copy Samuel at all.

sections.b:
1 Chronicles introduces the three Levite singers in two steps. For the ark's procession, the Levite leaders appoint Heman, Asaph and Ethan to sound bronze cymbals, with others on lyres and harps (15:16–22). At the ark's arrival, David puts Asaph in charge before the ark in Jerusalem (16:5, 16:37), while Heman and Jeduthun serve with Zadok at the tabernacle in Gibeon (16:41–42). The first thing they sing is a psalm of thanks built from Psalms 105, 96 and 106 (16:8–36), with the refrain "his loyal love is forever" (16:34; 16:41).

Ethan in chapter 15 and Jeduthun in chapter 16 hold the same place in the lists, and many readers take them as one man with two names, or Jeduthun as a later name for Ethan's guild. The singers' later division into twenty-four courses comes in chapter 25.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 15:16–24; 1 Chronicles 16:4–7; 1 Chronicles 16:37–42; 1 Chronicles 25:1–31; Psalm 39; Psalm 50; Psalm 88; Psalm 89

common: Chronicles credits David with founding the Temple's music, as later Jewish tradition did.
uncommon: Some scholars think the order of the singers (Heman first in chapter 15, Asaph first in chapter 16) reflects rivalry between singer guilds in the Second Temple.

sections.b:
Chronicles tells only Saul's last day. The account of his death on Gilboa follows 1 Samuel 31 closely, but Chronicles adds a judgment: "So Saul died for his unfaithfulness" (10:13). It names three failures: he did not keep the LORD's word, he went to a ghost of the dead for answers, and "He did not ask the LORD" (10:14). The first points back to Saul's disobedience at Gilgal and over Amalek (1 Samuel 13; 15); the second to the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28). The third is a hard reading, since 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul did ask and the LORD did not answer. Many readers think Chronicles means that Saul never truly sought God; the Hebrew uses two different verbs (sha'al in Samuel, darash in Chronicles).

Saul's house is said to have died together (10:6), though Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth lived. Chronicles speaks of the end of his dynasty, not of every descendant (compare 8:33–40).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:1–14; 1 Chronicles 8:33–40; 1 Samuel 13:13–14; 1 Samuel 15:22–28; 1 Samuel 28:6–19; 1 Samuel 31:1–13

common: Chronicles presents Saul as the model of the unfaithful king whose fall clears the way for David.

sections.b:
1 Chronicles 11–20 tells David's reign as a single rise. All Israel makes him king at once (11:1–3; 12:38). He takes Jerusalem (11:4–9) and seeks the ark first (13:3). Blessing follows: Hiram's builders, sons and victories (14). He organizes the Levites (15–16) and receives the promise of a lasting house (17). He wins on every side (18–20) and rules with "justice and righteousness" (18:14). The seven years of civil war, Bathsheba, Amnon, Absalom and Sheba are not told.

Readers explain the silence in three ways. Many critical scholars see an idealized David. Others see a focused portrait of the Temple's founder, written for readers who knew Samuel. Others again see a theological portrait of the forgiven king. Chronicles does include David's census and its punishment (21), and it says that David's wars disqualified him from building the Temple (22:8), so its David is not without fault.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:1–9; 1 Chronicles 12:38–40; 1 Chronicles 13:1–4; 1 Chronicles 17:1–27; 1 Chronicles 18:14; 1 Chronicles 20:1–3; 1 Chronicles 21:1–8

common: Chronicles leaves out David's sins with Bathsheba and Uriah because its subject is David as founder of worship and the Temple.
uncommon: Some scholars think Chronicles' readers were meant to read it alongside Samuel, as a commentary rather than a replacement.

sections.b:
1 Chronicles 20:1 copies the words that open the Bathsheba story in 2 Samuel 11:1, "But David was staying in Jerusalem," and then jumps to the end of the siege of Rabbah (2 Samuel 12:26–31). Bathsheba, Uriah, Nathan's parable and the death of the child are passed over. Bathsheba herself is named only once in Chronicles, as "Bath-shua," the mother of Solomon and three other sons (3:5).

Three views of the omission: (1) it cleans up David's image (Wellhausen and many since); (2) it is a choice of focus, since the private sins of David's house did not bear on the Temple, while the census did (Japhet, Williamson); (3) it reflects a theology of grace, in which David's repented sin no longer defines him. All three recognize that the readers knew the story from Samuel.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 20:1–3; 1 Chronicles 3:5; 2 Samuel 11:1; 2 Samuel 12:26–31; Psalm 51

uncommon: A few readers think Chronicles' abrupt join at 20:1 is deliberate, pointing readers to the story it does not tell.

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite," where 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan killed Goliath himself. The Hebrew of the two verses is very close. One view holds that Samuel's text was damaged and Chronicles keeps the original. Another holds that Chronicles, or its Samuel text, smoothed over a contradiction with 1 Samuel 17. A third, found in the Targum and some rabbis, identifies Elhanan with David. The verse shows how Chronicles can be both a witness to the text of Samuel and an interpreter of it.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 20:4–8; 2 Samuel 21:15–22; 1 Samuel 17:4–7; 1 Samuel 17:50

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 20:4–8 keeps three of the four giant stories of 2 Samuel 21:15–22. It leaves out the giant who nearly killed the aging David (2 Samuel 21:15–17). It calls these warriors "born to the Rapha in Gath" (20:8) and places the first among "one of the offspring of the Rephaim" (20:4). The Rephaim were the ancient tall peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20–21; Deuteronomy 3:11). One reading: Chronicles ends David's wars by finishing the conquest begun under Joshua.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 20:4–8; 2 Samuel 21:15–22; Deuteronomy 2:10–11; Deuteronomy 3:11; Joshua 11:21–22

sections.h: The ark comes to Jerusalem in Chronicles
sections.b: Chronicles makes the ark David's first concern as king (13:3) and splits its journey in two, with chapter 14 placed between the failed attempt (13) and the successful one (15–16). The reason for Uzzah's death is spelled out: he put his hand out to the ark (13:10), and the ark had not been carried by the Levites "the way the ruling requires" (15:13; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9). On the second attempt the Levites carry it on poles, the singers lead, and the ark is set in David's tent with a psalm of thanks (16:1–36). The tabernacle and its altar remain at Gibeon (16:39), so Israel has two places of worship until Solomon's Temple.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 13:1–14; 1 Chronicles 15:1–29; 1 Chronicles 16:1–6; 1 Chronicles 16:37–42; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9; 2 Samuel 6:1–19

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 15 is the first place in the story of the kings where the Levites act as a body. David declares that only they may carry the ark (15:2). He gathers six Levite clans, Kohath, Merari, Gershom, Elizaphan, Hebron and Uzziel (15:4–10), and tells them and the priests Zadok and Abiathar to make themselves holy (15:11–14). The Levites also become singers and gatekeepers (15:16–24; 16:4–6, 16:37–38). This is a Levitical ministry that Moses' law does not describe, and Chronicles presents it as David's adaptation of the old duty of carrying, once the ark has a resting place (compare 23:25–26).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 15:1–24; 1 Chronicles 16:4–6; 1 Chronicles 16:37–42; 1 Chronicles 23:25–32; Numbers 4:1–15; Deuteronomy 10:8

sections.b: When the ark arrives, David appoints Levites "to call him to mind, to give thanks, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel" (16:4). Praise becomes a daily, organized ministry alongside the sacrifices (16:37–42). The song of 16:8–36, taken from Psalms 105, 96 and 106, gives its content: remember God's covenant, call the nations to worship, and pray for rescue. Its refrain, "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; / his loyal love is forever" (16:34), returns at the dedication of the Temple (2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3) and at the founding of the second Temple (Ezra 3:11).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 16:4–42; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; Ezra 3:11; Psalm 105:1–15; Psalm 96:1–13; Psalm 106:1; Psalm 106:47–48

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 17 repeats 2 Samuel 7 with small but weighty changes. The son is promised a throne secure "for all time" (17:12). God says, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (17:13), but the warning about punishing him "with a rod such as men use" (2 Samuel 7:14) is missing. God will make him stand "in my house and in my kingdom" (17:14). The kingdom belongs to God, and David's son holds it under him. For readers after the exile, with no king, the promise was not lost but waiting. Later Jewish and Christian messianic hope drew on both versions (Psalm 89; Luke 1:32–33).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 17:1–27; 1 Chronicles 28:5–7; 1 Chronicles 29:23; 2 Samuel 7:1–29; Psalm 89:3–4; Luke 1:32–33

common: Chronicles removes the rod of correction because its Solomon is an obedient king.
uncommon: Some read 17:14 as pointing past Solomon to a future king, since Solomon's throne did not stand forever.

sections.b: Chronicles speaks of Israel's monarchy as God's own kingdom held in trust. The kingdom was "handed over" from Saul to David by the LORD (10:14; 12:23). David's son will stand "in my kingdom" (17:14). David knows that God has made his kingship great "for the good of his people Israel" (14:2). The model king seeks God, asks him before battle (14:10, 14:14) and rules with "justice and righteousness" (18:14).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:14; 1 Chronicles 12:23; 1 Chronicles 14:2; 1 Chronicles 17:14; 1 Chronicles 18:14; 1 Chronicles 28:5; 1 Chronicles 29:23

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 11:10–47 gives the list of David's warriors from 2 Samuel 23:8–39, but places it at the start of his reign and frames it with a new purpose: these men "stood firmly with him in his kingship, to make him king" (11:10). It adds sixteen names, several of them from east of the Jordan (11:41–47), and leaves out Samuel's note that Uriah is the last of thirty-seven. It then continues in chapter 12 with those who joined David at Ziklag and in the wilderness, including Amasai, on whom the Spirit came (12:18). The list is a key witness for restoring the damaged text of 2 Samuel 23.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:10–47; 1 Chronicles 12:1–22; 2 Samuel 23:8–39; 1 Chronicles 27:1–15

sections.b: "Then the Spirit put Amasai, chief of the Thirty, on like clothing" (12:18). The Hebrew says only ruach, "spirit," but most readers, and the Targum, take it as God's Spirit. The Hebrew idiom, the Spirit "clothed" a man, appears also for Gideon (Judges 6:34) and for Zechariah the priest (2 Chronicles 24:20). In each case the Spirit comes on someone suddenly to speak or act for God. Amasai's short poem of loyalty to David, "Peace, peace to you," is, on that reading, the Spirit's first word in Chronicles, and it is a word for David's kingdom.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 12:18; Judges 6:34; 2 Chronicles 24:20; 2 Chronicles 15:1; 2 Chronicles 20:14

sections.b: Chronicles tells the capture of Jerusalem right after the anointing (11:4–9), and it explains the old name: "Jerusalem, that is, Jebus" (11:4). It leaves out the hard saying about the blind and the lame (2 Samuel 5:6–8), adds that Joab won his command by leading the attack (11:6), and says that Joab restored the rest of the city (11:8). From here on Jerusalem is the center of the story, the place where the ark comes to rest (15:1) and, in chapter 21, where the Temple site is found.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:4–9; 2 Samuel 5:6–10; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; 1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1

sections.b: Chronicles gives Joab a better record than Samuel does. He becomes commander by leading the attack on Jebus (11:6) and restores the city (11:8). Before the battle with Ammon and Aram he speaks the words of faith, "The LORD will do whatever he sees is good" (19:13). He takes Rabbah (20:1), and in chapter 21 he resists the census. The murders of Abner and Amasa, the killing of Absalom and Joab's message about Uriah are not told.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:6–8; 1 Chronicles 18:15; 1 Chronicles 19:8–15; 1 Chronicles 20:1; 1 Chronicles 21:3–6; 2 Samuel 3:27; 2 Samuel 18:14

sections.h: Chronicles as a witness to Samuel
sections.b: Because Chronicles copied a Hebrew text of Samuel, it is one of the earliest witnesses to that text. In 1 Chronicles 10–20 it often agrees with the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a or the Greek against the Masoretic Text of Samuel. Examples include Baalah for Baale-judah (13:6), the reason for Uzzah's death (13:10), seven bulls and seven rams (15:26) and a thousand chariots (18:4). Elsewhere each book has its own slips: Chronicles skips a line in 11:13, and Samuel loses a word that Chronicles keeps (11:11). Comparing them shows that the text of Samuel was still varied in the Chronicler's day, around the fourth century BC.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:11–14; 1 Chronicles 13:6–10; 1 Chronicles 15:26; 1 Chronicles 18:4; 2 Samuel 6:2–7; 2 Samuel 8:4; 2 Samuel 23:8–12

sections.b: Several Masoretic notes in these chapters correct the written text. The "Thirty" and "officers" are confused (11:11; 12:18). The written "no name" is read "a name" (11:20; Hebrew lo' and lo). Hiram is read Huram (14:1), and Jaur is read Jair (20:5). The Plain English Translation follows the read form at 11:11, so that the list does not have two heads of the Thirty, and at 11:20 and 20:5, where the written form is likely a slip. It keeps the written form at 12:18 and 14:1. It also follows the read form without comment in a few names: Jeiel (11:44, written Jeuel), Jeziel (12:3, written Jezuel) and the Haruphite (12:5, written Hariphite).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 11:11; 1 Chronicles 11:20; 1 Chronicles 12:18; 1 Chronicles 14:1; 1 Chronicles 20:5

sections.b: Chronicles' version of Nathan's oracle promises: "I will not take my loyal love away from him, the way I took it from the one who was before you" (17:13), meaning Saul. The refrain of the Levites' song is "his loyal love is forever" (16:34; 16:41). In 19:2 David wants to "keep loyal love" with Hanun of Ammon because Hanun's father showed it to him. The insult that answers this kindness starts the war.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 16:34; 1 Chronicles 16:41; 1 Chronicles 17:13; 1 Chronicles 19:2; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3

sections.b: Chronicles says that after the ark came to Jerusalem, the tabernacle of Moses and its altar stayed "at the high place that was in Gibeon" (16:39), where Zadok and the priests kept the daily burnt offerings (16:40). Samuel and Kings do not mention this, though 1 Kings 3:4 calls Gibeon "the great high place." Chronicles uses it to explain why Solomon worshiped there (2 Chronicles 1:3–6) and why David did not go there in chapter 21 (21:29).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 16:39–42; 1 Chronicles 21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3–6; 1 Kings 3:4–5

sections.b: Chronicles never tells the story of Endor, but it names Saul's visit as one cause of his death: he went "to a ghost of the dead to ask for answers" (10:13). The word ov is the one used in 1 Samuel 28:7–8 and in the law forbidding necromancy (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11). Rabbinic midrash discusses Saul's visit to Endor at length (Leviticus Rabbah 26:7).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:13–14; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6; Deuteronomy 18:10–12

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 10–20 begins with a Philistine victory and ends with Philistine giants destroyed. In between, David twice asks God before fighting in the Valley of Rephaim (14:10, 14:14). He burns the idols the Philistines left behind (14:12), takes Gath and its villages (18:1), and his men kill the giants of Gath (20:4–8). The burning of the idols, where Samuel says David carried them off, is one of Chronicles' small corrections in line with the law (Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 7:25).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 10:1–10; 1 Chronicles 14:8–17; 1 Chronicles 18:1; 1 Chronicles 20:4–8; 2 Samuel 5:17–25; Deuteronomy 7:25

sections.b: Chronicles links David's wars to the Temple that Solomon would build. From Hadadezer's towns David took large amounts of bronze, which Solomon later used to make the bronze Sea, the pillars and the bronze objects (18:8). He also dedicated the gold, silver and bronze of the nations to the LORD (18:11). Nathan's oracle names David's son as the builder (17:12). Later, David tells Solomon that his own bloodshed kept him from building (22:8).
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 17:4–12; 1 Chronicles 18:8; 1 Chronicles 18:11; 1 Chronicles 22:8; 2 Samuel 8:8; 1 Kings 7:15–47

sections.b: 1 Chronicles 19–20 follows 2 Samuel 10 and 2 Samuel 12:26–31. Hanun humiliates David's envoys, Ammon hires Aramean chariots for a thousand talents of silver (19:6–7), Joab and Abishai defeat both armies, and Rabbah falls (20:1–3). Chronicles leaves out the story of Bathsheba and Uriah that Samuel sets inside this war. The treatment of the captives (20:3) is debated: the Hebrew of Chronicles reads "cut them with a saw," but most scholars restore Samuel's "set them to work," forced labor.
sections.refs: 1 Chronicles 19:1–19; 1 Chronicles 20:1–3; 2 Samuel 10:1–19; 2 Samuel 12:26–31
